items.title: CVE-2026-119977: WordPress WordPress Core Time-of-check Time-of-use (TOCTOU) Race Condition Vulnerability
items.detail: WordPress WordPress Core contains a time-of-check time-of-use (TOCTOU) race condition vulnerability that could allow unauthenticated attackers to execute code on the server during the upgrade window. This is due to predictable, web-accessible staging paths used during full-package core upgrades. Required action: Apply mitigations in accordance with vendor instructions, ensuring compliance with CISA’s BOD 26-04 Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk (see URL in Notes) guidance and CISA’s “Forensics Triage Requirements” (see URL in Notes). Follow applicable BOD 26-04 guidance for cloud services or discontinue use of the product if mitigations are unavailable. Stakeholders are responsible for evaluating each asset's internet exposure and ensuring adherence to BOD 26-04 patching guidelines. Catalog addition date is not the attack date.

items.title: Fake-download campaign uses trojanized installers to deliver monetization payloads
items.detail: In this article Attack chain overview Mitigation and protection guidance Learn More Microsoft Threat Intelligence has identified an evolving fake-download campaign targeting users searching for cracked commercial software, free games, activators, plugins, and unofficial utilities. The campaign uses trojanized Inno Setup-style installers to distribute multiple monetized software payloads, referred to by the delivery system as “offers”, during a single installation session. Our investigation found that the installers use a per-offer callback and status-tracking model to manage delivery and record installation outcomes. We confirmed three downstream monetization branches that transformed affected devices into monetized assets, including by routing third-party internet traffic through the device, enrolling it in a distributed-computing platform, or installing additional utility-style software, often without users’ informed knowledge or consent. These products and components may have legitimate uses, but their silent installation through deceptive software bundles without informed user consent introduces security and privacy risks. Organizations can reduce their exposure to this activity by preventing the use of untrusted software sources, enabling potentially unwanted application protection, and monitoring for unexpected software installations and persistence mechanisms. This blog details the campaign’s execution model and confirmed outcomes and provides mitigation guidance, Microsoft Defender protection information, advanced hunting queries, MITRE ATT&CK mappings, and indicators of compromise to help defenders identify, investigate, and respond to related activity. Attack chain overview The fake-download campaign follows a four-stage attack chain that progresses from deceptive lures through Inno-based staging, offer-controlled payload delivery, and installation of one or more monetization branches: Initial access via fake download lures – Users run fake installers promoted as cracked commercial software, free games, activators, plugins, executors, or unofficial utilities. Inno wrapper execution and temporary runner staging – The installer launches an Inno Setup-style temporary runner under %TEMP%\is-*.tmp\ , which starts recurring eld*.exe , set_*.exe , or other numbered stages. Offer execution callback and payload delivery – The runner contacts rotating infrastructure using a repeatable d=inno and r=offer_execution callback pattern. Offer, affiliate, download-network, placement, and session values coordinate downstream payload selection and correlate activity within the installer session. Final payload installation and monetization – Staged payloads use unattended installation switches to install one or more confirmed campaign branches: WorldProxyPool for proxy and network-resource monetization; CharityEngine and Berkeley Open Infrastructure for Network Computing (BOINC) for compute-resource monetization; or Advanced Windows (AW) Manager and Windows Manager for adware-style utility monetization. WorldProxyPool also creates recurring SYSTEM scheduled tasks for agent startup, watchdog execution, and updater activity. Attack Chain Figure 1. Overview of the attack chain. Initial access via fake download lures The campaign begins when users download and run fake installers promoted as cracked software, game installers, executors, activators, plugins, utilities, or driver and mobile-unlock tools. Observed lures include cracked audio plugins, PC games, Roblox executors, auto-clickers, driver tools, and fake utility installers. Example lures: Echo Client; FabFilter Total Bundle; Navicat Premium crack; Cue Club; auto-clicker; Deadpool Apunka Games; Command & Conquer: Red Alert 2; TFT Unlock Tool; and clownfishvoicechanger. Figure 2. Example utility download lure. Inno wrapper execution and temporary runner staging Across the investigated activity, user-launched lures spawned Inno Setup-style temporary runners under %TEMP%\is-*.tmp\ and then launched one or more numbered eld*.exe stages. Arguments such as /SL5 , /SPAWNWND , and /FIRSTWND , together with the temporary path and numbered stage names, provide more durable indicators than the original lure filename. The depth of the execution chain and its downstream outcome varied by installer session. One Echo Client example progressed through multiple numbered stages and reached several monetization branches, while other observed lures exposed fewer numbered stages or downstream components. The table below uses the Echo Client activity as a representative example of the wrapper-to-stage sequence; individual installer sessions may launch different combinations of numbered stages. Step Process Command-line / path signal Role 1 Echo Client.exe Launched from %USERPROFILE%\Downloads\Echo Client\ User-launched lure 2 Echo Client.tmp %TEMP%\is-*.tmp\… with /SL5=… Inno temporary runner 3 Echo Client.exe /SPAWNWND=… /FIRSTWND=… Inno child process / window handoff 4 Echo Client.tmp /SL5=… /SPAWNWND=… /FIRSTWND=… Temporary runner continues execution 5 eld*.exe eld0.exe , eld1.exe , eld3.exe , eld4.exe , and eld5.exe under %TEMP%\is-*.tmp\ Numbered staged payloads Table 1. Inno wrapper execution and temporary runner staging. Offer execution callback and payload delivery After staging, the Inno temporary runner contacted rotating callback infrastructure using randomized URL paths but a repeatable query-string structure: http:// / ?sis= &fz= &d=inno&r=offer_execution&ko=no&o= &a= &dn= &spot= &t= &cr= Failed or blocked offers used r=offer_execution_fail and sometimes included local error text, including messages that the operation did not complete because the file contained a virus or potentially unwanted software. These callbacks are useful campaign-attribution and sequencing markers, but they are not always the earliest prevention point. In some endpoint detection and response (EDR) traces, child payloads launched before or around the r=offer_execution callback. The campaign used offer IDs, affiliate IDs, download-network IDs, and placement values to select or report downstream payload attempts. Observed offer and download-network combinations included o=1712 / dn=507 , o=1720 / dn=536 , o=1727 / dn=564 , o=1729 / dn=566 , o=331 / dn=244 , o=1674 / dn=440 , o=1675 / dn=441 , o=1681 / dn=447 , and o=1730 / dn=567 . Different offers could succeed or fail independently within the same installer session, so a failed first offer did not necessarily mean that the full bundle stopped. Parameter Observed use Assessment d Often set to inno Installer or delivery-family marker sis Stable within an installer session Session-correlation value a Stable across related requests Affiliate, campaign, or distribution-partner identifier o Changes by offer Offer identifier dn / on Changes with the offer or retrieval path Download-network or offer-network field; exact meaning unconfirmed spot Increments through the session Offer placement, slot, or execution order paw Present across offer requests Request, package, or session-correlation value; exact meaning unconfirmed fz Present in outcome callbacks Delivered package size or file-size field t Present in outcome callbacks Timing, token, or request value; exact meaning unconfirmed r offer_execution or offer_execution_fail Per-offer execution result msg Present on failed offers Error text from the local download or installation attempt ko / cr Boolean-like or short values Server-side control or result flags; exact meaning unconfirmed Table 2. Assessments are based on observed telemetry correlations, not confirmed server-side definitions. Offer / download-network pair Semantic meaning o=1712 / dn=507 Primary first-stage offer commonly attempted at the start of the installer flow. o=1720 / dn=536 Offer branch associated with CharityEngine/BOINC distributed-compute monetization. o=1727 / dn=564 Offer branch associated with WorldProxyPool proxyware monetization. o=1729 / dn=566 Recurring follow-on offer branch in the installer flow. o=331 / dn=244 Secondary offer branch observed in the multi-offer sequence. o=1674 / dn=440 Later campaign offer branch. o=1675 / dn=441 Low-volume offer branch. o=1681 / dn=447 Additional offer branch in the campaign’s installer rotation. o=1730 / dn=567 Later high-volume offer branch. Table 3. Offer and download-network pairs and their semantic roles in the installer flow. The campaign rotated callback domains frequently while preserving the same d=inno and offer-execution callback structure across recurring lure categories. Individual domains are therefore short-lived infrastructure indicators; the durable hunting signal is the combination of the callback pattern, Inno temporary execution, staged filenames, and related installer-session activity. The full observed domain set is provided in the IOC section. Final payload installation and monetization After offer callback and payload delivery, the campaign launched downstream installers or components using unattended installation switches such as /qn , /S , /quiet , and /norestart . This stage converted the fake-download execution chain into installed software and recurring execution across three monetization branches: proxy and network-resource monetization, compute-resource monetization, and adware-style utility monetization. Branch Primary behavior Representative artifacts A. WorldProxyPool Proxy agent installation and scheduled-task setup sdk-agent.exe; sdk-agent.updater.exe; watchdog.ps1; WorldProxyPoolAgent task B. CharityEngine / BOINC Distributed-compute software installation boinc.exe; charityengine.exe; ce11.exe; VirtualBox-7.2.8-r173730.msi C. AW Manager / Windows Manager Utility and updater-style software installation Windows Manager – Postback Johan.msi; AdvancedWindowsManager.exe; Windows Updater.exe Table 4. Summary of the three monetization branches and representative artifacts. Proxy and network-resource monetization — WorldProxyPool In the WorldProxyPool branch, a staged eld4.exe payload created three SYSTEM-level scheduled tasks for components under C:\Program Files\WorldProxyPool\ . WorldProxyPoolAgent configured sdk-agent.exe to run at system startup with highest privileges; WorldProxyPoolWatchdog configured a hidden, noninteractive PowerShell watchdog script to run every five minutes; and WorldProxyPoolUpdater configured sdk-agent.updater.exe update to run hourly. The installer also started the agent task immediately with schtasks.exe /Run . Subsequent task launches were brokered by the Windows Task Scheduler service ( svchost.exe -k netsvcs -p -s Schedule ), causing sdk-agent.exe and the watchdog script to execute in the service context. This persistence mechanism supports recurring proxy-agent, watchdog, and updater activity, consistent with network-resource monetization. Scheduled task Purpose WorldProxyPoolAgent Runs sdk-agent.exe at system startup as SYSTEM with highest privileges; the installer also started it immediately with schtasks.exe /Run . WorldProxyPoolWatchdog Runs a hidden, noninteractive PowerShell watchdog script every five minutes as SYSTEM with highest privileges. WorldProxyPoolUpdater Runs sdk-agent.updater.exe update hourly as SYSTEM with highest privileges. Table 5. WorldProxyPool scheduled tasks created during the proxyware installation chain Figure 3. WorldProxyPool installation and persistence. eld4.exe created SYSTEM-level startup, five-minute watchdog, and hourly updater tasks. Compute-resource monetization — CharityEngine and BOINC In the CharityEngine and BOINC branch, the offer payload installed distributed-compute software and supporting components under C:\Program Files\BOINC\ and C:\ProgramData\BOINC\ . Observed components included ce-installer_7.14.2_vbox-7.2.8.exe , ce_7.14.2_windows_x86_64.exe , charityengine.exe , boinc.exe , boinctray.exe , boinc.scr , boincscr.exe , wrapper_2022110901_windows_x86_64.exe , ce11.exe , and VirtualBox-7.2.8-r173730.msi . They covered BOINC launch, compute-wrapper execution, GPU or compute-capability checks, CharityEngine project communication, and VirtualBox installation. Figure 4. CharityEngine/BOINC compute-monetization branch. Adware-style utility monetization: AdvancedWindowsManager / Windows Manager The same Inno offer-execution infrastructure delivered an AW Manager or Windows Manager branch. In one observed process tree, the Inno runner spawned eld3.exe , launched Windows Manager – Postback Johan.msi , and installed AdvancedWindowsManager.exe and Windows Updater.exe under paths resembling %APPDATA%\AW Manager\Windows Manager 1.0.0\ or C:\Program Files (x86)\AW Manager\Windows Manager\ . Figure 5. AW Manager / Windows Manager utility-install branch. Mitigation and protection guidance Microsoft recommends the following actions to reduce exposure to this campaign and detect related activity: Preventive controls Avoid untrusted software sources. Do not download cracked software, key generators, unofficial game installers, or software activation tools, which are common delivery mechanisms for malware, potentially unwanted applications, and monetization campaigns. Enable cloud-delivered protection. Verify that Microsoft Defender Antivirus cloud-delivered protection is enabled to improve detection of emerging malware and potentially unwanted applications. See: Configure cloud-delivered protection Keep tamper protection enabled. Use tamper protection to help prevent unauthorized changes to Microsoft Defender security settings. See: Learn about tamper protection . Enable reputation-based protection. Configure reputation-based protection to help block known malicious and untrusted applications and downloads. See: Configure reputation-based protection . Consider Attack Surface Reduction (ASR) protections. Evaluate ASR rules, including rules that block executable files unless they meet prevalence, age, or trusted-list criteria. See: Review Attack Surface Reduction rules . Investigation actions Investigate execution from Inno temporary directories. Review activity from paths such as %TEMP%\is-*.tmp\ , particularly when staged executables such as eld*.exe , set_*.exe , FirstFast[1].exe , or SecondRunner[1].exe are observed. Correlate Inno callback activity. Monitor outbound requests containing d=inno together with r=offer_execution or r=offer_execution_fail, and review related process, file, and network activity across the complete installer session. Review unexpected scheduled tasks. Investigate newly created scheduled tasks, particularly tasks running with SYSTEM privileges or recurring watchdog and updater functions. See: Audit scheduled task creation events . Audit software inventory for unexpected installations. Review endpoints for the presence of software such as WorldProxyPool, CharityEngine, BOINC, VirtualBox, or other applications that users did not intentionally install. See: Review software inventory in Defender Vulnerability Management . Microsoft Defender XDR detections Microsoft Defender detects and blocks campaign-linked payloads through cloud protection, machine-learning classifications, network inspection, and behavior monitoring. Relevant observed detections include remote-thread injection, scheduled-task launch, and suspicious outbound HTTP activity. Customers with provisioned access can also use Microsoft Security Copilot in Microsoft Defender to investigate and respond to incidents, hunt for threats, and protect their organization with relevant threat intelligence. Tactic Observed activity Microsoft Defender coverage Initial access and execution Users execute fake cracked-software installers, including files presented as Navicat Premium or FabFilter bundles, from Downloads, archive-extraction folders, or Inno extraction paths. The installers launch temporary payloads from %TEMP%\is-*.tmp\. Microsoft Defender Antivirus – Trojan:Win64/OfferLoader.DA!MTB – Trojan:Win64/OfferLoader.DB!MTB Microsoft Defender for Endpoint – A suspicious file was observed – An active ‘Wacatac’ malware was detected – ‘Kepavll’ malware was prevented Command and control / campaign tracking Outbound callbacks use a stable Inno offer-execution URL contract: d=inno with r=offer_execution or r=offer_execution_fail . Each callback reports an individual offer result. Correlating these callbacks with process, file, network, persistence, and installation events provides visibility across the multi-offer session. Microsoft Defender Antivirus – Behavior:Win32/SuspInnoOffer.A!mapsi Microsoft Defender for Endpoint – Suspicious ‘SuspInnoOffer’ behavior was blocked Staging and payload delivery The installer chain drops multiple staged files from Inno temporary directories, commonly named eld*.exe , set_*.exe , FirstFast[1].exe , and SecondRunner[1].exe . Microsoft Defender Antivirus – Trojan:Win64/OfferLoader.DA!MTB – Trojan:Win64/OfferLoader.DB!MTB Microsoft Defender for Endpoint – A suspicious file was observed – An active ‘Wacatac’ malware was detected – An active ‘Egairtigado’ malware was blocked – ‘Kepavll’ malware was prevented Persistence In the investigated Navicat chain, WorldProxyPool created SYSTEM scheduled tasks with highest privileges: WorldProxyPoolAgent at startup, WorldProxyPoolWatchdog every five minutes through hidden noninteractive PowerShell, and WorldProxyPoolUpdater hourly. It also wrote uninstall metadata under the WorldProxyPool registry key. Microsoft Defender for Endpoint – Suspicious scheduled task activity – Suspicious Scheduled Task Process Launched – Suspicious Task Scheduler activity Resource hijacking / monetization Two monetization paths were confirmed. The Navicat chain installed WorldProxyPool proxyware. The FabFilter chain silently installed CharityEngine/BOINC, VirtualBox, and Visual C++ components, launched BOINC workloads, and contacted CharityEngine infrastructure. Microsoft Defender Antivirus – Adware:Win32/Clover – Trojan:Win64/OfferLoader.DA!MTB – Trojan:Win64/OfferLoader.DB!MTB Microsoft Defender for Endpoint – An active ‘Clover’ malware was detected – An active ‘Wacatac’ malware was detected Defense evasion and suspicious behavior Several staged payloads are associated with defense-evasion, execution, persistence, remote-thread, and other suspicious behaviors. Microsoft Defender Antivirus – Trojan:Win32/OffLoader.A Microsoft Defender for Endpoint – Suspicious ‘SuspEtherRpcConn’ behavior was blocked – Suspicious ‘SuspSmsScanConn’ behavior was blocked Microsoft Security Copilot Security Copilot customers can use the standalone experience to create their own prompts or run prebuilt promptbooks to automate investigation and response tasks related to this campaign. Useful promptbooks include: Incident investigation Microsoft User analysis Threat actor profile Threat Intelligence 360 report based on MDTI intelligence Vulnerability impact assessment. Some promptbooks require access to Microsoft Defender XDR, Microsoft Sentinel, or related Microsoft security plugins. For this campaign, analysts can prompt Security Copilot to summarize and correlate available incident evidence, subject to connected data and permissions. Threat intelligence reports Microsoft customers can use Microsoft Defender XDR Threat analytics and related Microsoft threat intelligence reporting to track this rotating, multi-offer fake-download campaign and review updates on its Inno callbacks, offer outcomes, staged payloads, infrastructure, and proxyware or distributed-compute results. The reporting helps analysts correlate offer callbacks and endpoint activity from the same installer session, identify devices with associated monetization stages, and assess the overall bundle outcome. It also provides investigation context, protection guidance, relevant indicators, and recommended response actions. Advanced hunting Microsoft Defender XDR customers can run the following advanced hunting queries to find related activity in their networks. Inno offer-execution callbacks DeviceNetworkEvents | where RemoteUrl has "d=inno" | where RemoteUrl has_any ("r=offer_execution", "r=offer_execution_fail") | project Timestamp, DeviceName, RemoteUrl, InitiatingProcessFileName Payload execution from Inno temporary directories DeviceProcessEvents | where FolderPath has @"\AppData\Local\Temp\is-" | where FileName matches regex @"(?i)^(eld[0-9]+|set_[0-9]+|FirstFast(?:\[1\])?|SecondRunner(?:\[1\])?)\.exe$" | project Timestamp, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName, SHA256 Outbound connections to observed campaign infrastructure DeviceNetworkEvents | where RemoteUrl has_any ("orbittrack.cfd", "prairielink.cfd", "willowbox.xyz", "stonestation.cfd", "foldlodge.xyz", "friendsanchor.xyz", "fallport.cfd", "wishcourt.cfd", "cratebase.cfd", "belieftrack.cfd", "beliefdesk.xyz", "companyharbor.xyz", "signalpane.cfd", "inkact.xyz", "wishgrove.cfd") | project Timestamp, DeviceName, RemoteUrl, RemotePort, InitiatingProcessFileName Hunting note: Treat each callback as an individual offer result. Group events by device, time window, and available session or affiliate fields, then correlate the callbacks with Inno temporary execution, staged filenames, scheduled-task creation, and monetization-software activity. Domain-only matches are leads, not confirmation. Validate the queries against the current Microsoft Defender XDR schema before publication. MITRE ATT&CK Techniques observed The following MITRE ATT&CK mappings reflect behaviors observed in the investigated activity. Mappings are limited to evidence described in this report. Execution T1204.002 User Execution: Malicious File | A user launches an installer presented as cracked software, a game, an activator, a plugin, or an unofficial utility. Persistence T1053.005 Scheduled Task/Job: Scheduled Task | WorldProxyPool creates SYSTEM-level startup, watchdog, and updater tasks; the watchdog runs every five minutes and the updater runs hourly. Defense evasion T1036 Masquerading | Installers are presented with names and branding associated with cracked commercial software or unofficial software bundles to encourage execution. T1564.003 Hide Artifacts: Hidden Window | The WorldProxyPool watchdog invokes PowerShell with hidden, noninteractive execution options. Command and control T1071.001 Application Layer Protocol: Web Protocols | The installer sends HTTP callbacks to rotating infrastructure using the durable d=inno and r=offer_execution or r=offer_execution_fail query pattern. T1105 Ingress Tool Transfer | The campaign retrieves staged executables and supporting components from threat actor-controlled, cloud-storage, and content delivery network (CDN)-hosted locations. Impact T1496 Resource Hijacking | The campaign installs CharityEngine/BOINC for distributed computing and WorldProxyPool for proxyware monetization, abusing victim compute and network resources through deceptive bundled installation. For standard industry documentation about these techniques, refer to the MITRE ATT&CK framework . Indicators of compromise (IOC) The following indicators of compromise (IOCs) were observed during investigation of this campaign and can assist defenders in identifying related activity and conducting threat-hunting efforts. Indicator Type Component beliefdesk[.]xyz Domain Offer-execution callback infrastructure. companyharbor[.]xyz Domain Offer-execution callback infrastructure. signalpane[.]cfd Domain Offer-execution callback infrastructure. inkact[.]xyz Domain Offer-execution callback infrastructure. wishgrove[.]cfd Domain Offer-execution callback infrastructure. %TEMP%\is-*.tmp\eld*.exe File path Recurring staged payload naming and path pattern. C:\Program Files\WorldProxyPool\sdk-agent.exe File path WorldProxyPool proxyware component. items.title: Microsoft named a Leader in the 2026 Gartner® Magic Quadrant™ for AI Agent Management Platforms
items.detail: Microsoft has been named a Leader in the inaugural 2026 Gartner® Magic Quadrant™ for AI Agent Management Platforms . We believe this recognition reflects Microsoft’s approach to helping organizations manage, secure, and scale their AI investments through Microsoft Agent 365 . Figure 1: Gartner, Magic Quadrant for AI Agent Management Platforms, October 27, 2026. Monitor and manage agents with Microsoft Agent 365 When we introduced Agent 365, we started with a simple concept: agents should be managed with the same rigor you already apply to users, apps, and devices, using the infrastructure and protections that already run your business. Since then, more than 50 million agents have been registered in Agent 365. 1 Here’s what we believe made the difference. We started with identity, not monitoring Many approaches to managing agents focus on monitoring after an agent is running. Microsoft’s approach begins with identity. With Microsoft Entra Agent ID , every agent in the organization is assigned a unique agent ID, associated with an owner and purpose, and the right access controls based on its needs. This enables organizations to apply established identity and access policies to both people and agents. Agent access policies are dynamically adjusted as risk signals and conditions change. Organizations can manage agent access through the Microsoft identity infrastructure they already use for their workforce. We built on what you already trust Rather than building a separate platform, Agent 365 extends the tools IT and security teams already use every day: Microsoft Entra, Microsoft Defender, Microsoft Purview, Microsoft Intune, and the Microsoft 365 admin center. That decision shapes the experience. Microsoft data protection, compliance, and security capabilities can help organizations extend familiar controls to supported agent scenarios. 2 We meet agents where they are Agents won’t come from one platform, so Agent 365 is designed to support a broad ecosystem. It brings supported agents from Microsoft, customer-built agents, local agents found on devices, and partner clouds and frameworks into one registry. Current integrations include Agentforce, Amazon Bedrock, Anthropic, Databricks, Google Gemini, and Google Vertex, with more planned integrations coming soon, including OpenAI, ServiceNow, and Snowflake. Agent 365 also integrates agents built using supported open-source frameworks with the Agent 365 software development kit (SDK). For additional agent patterns, including local and previously unknown agents discovered through Microsoft Security sensors, Agent 365 supports fit-for-purpose identity types so they can be represented in the registry with appropriate ownership, activity, and risk context. Microsoft is also previewing discovery of cloud agents, extending visibility beyond known and integrated agents. Together, native integrations, connectors, and security sensors help organizations discover and govern more of their agent estate across cloud and device environments. There’s more to do Agent 365 moved quickly from introduction to general availability, and we haven’t slowed down. We’re proud of this recognition, and we know there’s more work ahead. We are expanding discovery to 35 additional local agent types, bringing the total to 60, along with adding support to discover unknown agents, bringing these agents under management, as well as extending policy coverage and controls for both managed and unmanaged agents, including third-party agents. But, visibility and controls are only the beginning. Customers have asked for more automated support for agent governance and security. The new Agent 365 Action Center helps IT and security leaders move from reactive alerts to prescriptive actions, like cleaning up inactive agents, reassigning ownerless agents, or automatically blocking agents based on risk. We’re also advancing cost management, task classification, and value calculation to help organizations understand how agents are being used, what they cost, and the value they deliver. Our promise hasn’t changed: to help every organization move from experimenting with agents to running them confidently, with the same rigor, protections, and accountability that already run the enterprise. We believe Agent 365 enables any organization to deploy AI at scale. Get started Get your copy of the Gartner Magic Quadrant for AI Agent Management Platforms . Learn more about Microsoft Agent 365 . Get Agent 365 with Microsoft 365 E7 , or as an add-on to Microsoft 365 E5. Attending Microsoft Ignite 2026? Join us to learn more about what’s next for Agent 365. Get started with Microsoft Agent 365 To learn more about Microsoft Security solutions, visit our website. Bookmark the Security blog to keep up with our expert coverage on security matters. Also, follow us on LinkedIn ( Microsoft Security ) and X ( @MSFTSecurity ) for the latest news and updates on cybersecurity. items.title: MLEP in KICS for Networks 5.0: how machine learning helps track network behavior of OT devices
items.detail: In an industrial network, malicious activity can be hard to tell apart from normal data exchange between devices. Malicious actors routinely rely on legitimate tools and the Living-off-the-Land technique, so a single network connection may show no known signs of an attack: the device uses a familiar protocol and transmits ordinary data. An anomaly can hide in subtle details: the data source, the time of access, or the volume of transferred data may be atypical for a particular device. However, to detect this kind of anomaly, you need to understand the roles of the devices at both ends of the connection and know which network activity patterns are typical for them. But an organization’s asset inventory data is often incomplete, which makes it harder to catch unauthorized connections in time. Suppose monitoring detects a host that regularly exchanges data with programmable logic controllers (PLCs). Its IP address is known, but the inventory does not specify what role it plays: is it an engineering workstation, a process data server, or a piece of contractor’s equipment? The host may also have been on the industrial network for a long time, with its record going out of date after a network upgrade. In the joint OT asset inventory guidance released by CISA and its partners in 2025 , inventorying devices and classifying them by role are treated as part of OT asset management. For organizations, this is one of the most important areas: according to the SANS 2025 ICS security survey , 50% of respondents had deployed or significantly expanded ICS inventory and visibility tools over the previous 12 months, and 54% named them as investment priorities for the next 12–24 months. Device inventory in Kaspersky Industrial CyberSecurity for Networks In Kaspersky Industrial CyberSecurity for Networks , the Asset Discovery technology is the foundation of asset visibility. Passive network traffic analysis detects devices and their interactions, while recognition rules help determine the device category and extract available information about it, such as the vendor, model, or software version. Exactly which attributes the system can obtain depends on the protocol and the traffic it observes. We covered this in more detail at the Kaspersky Industrial Cybersecurity Conference . Hardware and software information in the device card The product also supports active polling modules (APMs): where polling is allowed, they can request additional configuration and firmware version details from devices. This kind of inventory is far more detailed than a list of IP addresses. Installed modules and their placement in a PLC rack However, even accurate hardware information doesn’t always explain what function a host performs in a specific industrial facility. Gaps appear for various reasons. Some devices send identifying information only at startup or during configuration, while others rarely communicate. Proprietary protocols can’t always be parsed, and encryption may leave only connection metadata for analysis. If the monitoring system doesn’t receive traffic from every segment of the industrial network, some network activity goes unobserved. Active polling doesn’t suit every device or every operating condition. Devices of unknown category When there isn’t enough direct information about a device, its category can be refined by looking at the patterns of its recurring network interactions. Analyzing these interactions is the job of Machine Learning Event Processor (MLEP), a service included in Kaspersky Industrial CyberSecurity for Networks 5.0. This machine-learning-based event processor can both refine device categories and detect anomalies in their network behavior. What data does MLEP analyze? To compare device behavior, you don’t need to store every packet as a separate observation (a data object) in the ML model. MLEP represents network sessions as a sequence of short 15-second fragments. For each fragment, MLEP stores information about the endpoints (IP, MAC, and port), the direction of data exchange, the protocol, and the number and size of the packets transmitted. Together these make up an event , which then gets a timestamp. Traffic thus becomes a sequence of events showing which hosts a device communicated with, when, and how communication intensity changed. Aggregating data into events also sets the method’s limits. An aggregated fragment can’t be used to reconstruct the exact order of individual packets or the content of commands. MLEP can draw conclusions about a new protocol only if another KICS technology has managed to recognize it. That said, comparing stable network connections and changes in exchange volume doesn’t require a detailed record of every packet. These observations form the basis of the device’s behavioral history. From observations to MLEP results Each object has its own behavioral history, and one object’s history can’t be applied to another. But the principles of behavior analysis, along with some common rules, work across different objects. Let’s look at how this works in MLEP, which is built on a spiking neural semantic network (NSN). Event identification Neurosemantic networks structure information as a multilayer ordered graph, where the data in each consecutive layer builds on the data in the previous one. The nodes of this graph — that is, the units of information in each layer — act as neurons.The NSN creates dedicated channels to handle different event parameters (port, IP, and so on). Unique parameter values for each channel are stored as neurons in layer 0. The event itself, which consists of a set of parameter values, is stored as a neuron in layer 1 of the network. If an event occurs for the first time, neurogenesis creates a new neuron with input connections to the corresponding parameter neurons. This lets the network learn and operate on the event stream at the same time. If the event has occurred before, the network activates the same neuron that was created when the event first appeared. This way, the network identifies each event precisely. Each neuron that corresponds to an event also collects basic statistics: when it was last activated and how many times it has been activated. Event history In NSN-based event processing, layer 2 and above store sequences of events over time: recurring patterns and the full history. However, categorization and statistical anomaly detection don’t require storing the full packet sequence or a detailed timeline of every network event. As we noted earlier, events are themselves aggregates, which means the order of network packets has already been averaged out. So MLEP keeps history only temporarily, within each episode (30,000 aggregated events by default), which saves computing resources. Statistics processing in MLEP MLEP processes statistics mainly through specialized listener neurons on layer −1 (minus one) of the network. Attention heads and monitors are built on these neurons. Key components of the NSN When an event arrives, the corresponding neuron is activated, and the network instantly knows whether that neuron is new or was created earlier. Each attention head subscribes to the events or event features it needs and takes in only the activations of the matching neurons. If an event occurs for the first time, all heads are notified and then decide whether to subscribe (grow a connection to the relevant neuron) and receive information about activations of such neurons from then on. It is called a spiking network because activation information is a spike, not a number. This spike tells the head that something it’s interested in has happened. An attention head is configured according to scenarios — the situations that MLEP should send alerts about. The core of a head’s configuration is a query, which filters incoming information and serves as the subscription criterion. Unlike regular database queries, this query runs on the stream, so it can react to an event instantly. Attention heads work very much like the semantics of ordinary human language. A query has a subject of attention (one or more grammatical subjects) and conditions (the other parts of the sentence). In the infrastructure of an industrial enterprise, the subjects are devices on the network, and the conditions are various aspects of network communication, such as ports, protocol, and average packet size. If a head has many subjects (for example, if it’s interested in every device on an industrial network), it fans out: it creates a child head for each individual value of the subject of attention, that is, each device. The child head then watches a specific device and reports to the parent head. Attention heads don’t accumulate or process statistics. They only filter event streams. When an attention head receives a relevant event, it activates and sends a spike to the monitor subscribed to that head. Monitors, in turn, have stacks for accumulating and processing events. They can also have their own queries and post-filter information from the head. For example, they can select only new events from those filtered by the head. There are several types of monitors: Stat monitors track changes in the average count of specific events (for example, device activity) over time intervals typical for those events, or in the average values of numeric event parameters (for example, changes in device traffic volume). Monitors work from the event alone: they fire when an event has occurred a certain number of times within a given interval, or has occurred for the first time. Similar-behavior monitors work with heads that can generalize events, that is, extract just a few parameters whose combination is shared (generalized) across many events. MLEP uses these monitor types to implement scenarios for categorizing devices and detecting their anomalous behavior: For categorization, MLEP uses attention heads and monitors that identify common behavior across different assets and group devices accordingly. MLEP then takes information from Asset Discovery about the known categories of some assets and extends those categories to other assets in the same group. Because a device can show different types of activity, it may land in several groups. MLEP then makes a weighted assessment across all relevant groups. Groups of devices with similar network behavior At the final stage, the system verifies that assigning the category to the asset is permissible. This is again done by special rule monitors loaded into the NSN at system startup. The rules rely on asset metadata available from Asset Discovery and APMs. MLEP takes a similar approach to anomaly detection: an attention head and a monitor define an anomaly scenario, often loosely. When a monitor activates on such a scenario, MLEP generates an alert about unusual behavior. The current version of MLEP ships with preconfigured heads and monitors. The functional dynamic diagram below shows how events from devices on an industrial network are processed. Event processing flow (click to play) MLEP in practice: how behavior helps complete the asset inventory At a facility with several similar production lines, device information may be more complete on some lines than on others. On one line, devices are identified as PLCs, while on another, after an upgrade, some hosts show up only as addresses: the available traffic didn’t provide enough information to determine their category. Still, these devices communicate with the same types of HMIs and process data collection servers. Their communication directions, frequency, and volumes may be similar. That’s where MLEP comes in. It takes the categories of already known assets and matches recurring features of their network behavior against those of uncategorized devices. When the observed interactions turn out to be similar, MLEP can add a category for that host to the inventory. Device category suggested by MLEP Once the category is refined, the industrial network map provides more context about the equipment on the network. When analyzing network activity, the analyst immediately sees the device’s suggested category and can skip looking up each IP address in the design diagrams. This approach is especially useful where equipment changes faster than the documentation is updated. The suggested category is also checked against existing device information and defined constraints. This helps filter out some contradictory options, but prediction quality still depends on how much of the traffic is visible, especially if the device communicates only rarely. Anomalous activity and streaming statistics Investigations of real-world attacks show that attackers actively use both standard tools and permitted protocols. You don’t always need to know an attacker’s specific technique in advance to spot potentially malicious activity. Signature-based detection helps find known signs of an attack, but it doesn’t assess how typical an observed interaction is for a particular device. MLEP compares current activity with the device’s usual network profile: which hosts it communicates with, which protocols it uses, when and how much data it transmits, its average packet size, and so on. The changes it detects help guide the direction of the investigation. Correlating these changes with other events and the operational context helps determine whether malicious actions could be behind them. When investigating an incident that has already been detected, anomalies help reconstruct the sequence of actions. The first version of MLEP comes with six preconfigured monitors, one for each type of deviation from the device’s usual network profile: Anomaly How it helps with event analysis New external host Flags a new external connection that wasn’t previously seen in the device’s observed behavior, even if the IP address isn’t listed among known IoCs. Helps check whether this connection appeared at the same time as other suspicious events. New combination of destination address and port Shows that the device has begun using a service it hasn’t used before. Once an incident has been detected, this helps trace new connections after the more critical events have been analyzed. Unusually large volume of data sent Highlights data transfers that are atypical for the device and helps correlate their timing and direction with other events. Atypical activity time Shows that the device was active at a time that’s unusual for it. In an already detected incident, this helps reconstruct the timeline of actions around the main alert. New protocol Helps spot a new method of communication, even when the device is communicating with familiar hosts. Activity with signs of scanning Shows that the device has started contacting an unusually large number of neighboring hosts. This signal helps reveal possible reconnaissance ahead of attempts to access equipment. During an investigation, anomalies help reconstruct the sequence of changes: when a specific host established new connections, switched protocols, increased its data transfer volume, or shifted its operating hours. Matching events by device and time shows an analyst how activity unfolded around an incident that has already been detected. This is especially useful when some of the attacker’s actions fell outside the monitored scope or didn’t trigger other KICS technologies. Correlating these changes with the device’s role, protocol analysis data, and events from other technologies gives the analyst a more complete timeline. Behavioral anomalies show exactly where to look for the missing links and which network interactions need attention. Atypical Activity Time anomaly card In the event list, anomalies detected by MLEP are marked with an AI label. Each event shows its name, source, destination, timestamp, and the ID of the triggered scenario. Conclusion In an industrial network, whether behavior is anomalous depends on the host where it occurs and that host’s place in the industrial process. The repetitive nature of many communications makes a change in normal data exchange easier to spot, while knowing a device’s function and criticality helps gauge the possible consequences. Taken together, these observations make network traffic more than a list of connections: it helps assess new events in the context of a specific facility, even without an attack scenario known in advance. Machine learning technologies are well suited to this kind of comprehensive analysis, as they can process and organize huge streams of heterogeneous data. Starting with version 5.0, Kaspersky Industrial CyberSecurity for Networks handles this function with MLEP, which works effectively alongside the product’s existing functionality.
